title: Bowing in jazz and Slam Stewart
summary: Jazz bassists are now expected to bow a chorus; Mazzari recalls being scorned for it years ago and notes today's bowers do not simply imitate Slam Stewart.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: What about bowling now? Do the jazz musicians bow like the legit men?

Well, they have to now, you know. Practically every bass player is expected to bow a chorus, and that's where a good bass player is, can be picked out. I mean, well, you gotta know how to hold your bow, and you gotta know how to phrase your notes with the left hand and the coordination of the two hands. And I'm glad, I'm glad, I'm so glad to see that because years ago I used to try in bow courses and guys used to just laugh at me, you know? I'm so glad to see that now that practically, well, I won't say practically all of it, but a lot of tunes, now they give a bass player a bowing lick, you know, which is real nice. When was it that you bowed? Oh, it was quite a few years ago. I tried in different bands and I got kind of scorned that so I didn't try it anymore, you know?
was very popular with it in the...

And in those days, I think that they were just saying, well, man, who do you think you are imitating Slam Stewart? Like, so these guys today, they're imitating Slam Stewart? No, they don't sound at all like Slam Stewart. They have their own individual way of playing. So I'm glad to see that. I think it's real nice. I could hear two choruses of it. Don't worry about that.
